passage:
Aparna, can I tell you something ugly? Every first of the month, when my salary comes, I send most of it home. Nanu's house repairs, my brother's college fees, the old loan. I do it gladly. Mostly.
But last week the admission letter for the evening design course came, and I just sat on the bus holding it. I couldn't afford it. Again. And I felt this flash of, why is it always me? Then straight away I felt terrible for thinking that about the people who raised me.
So I did something new. I called Maa, and instead of saying 'all fine', I said, 'Maa, I love you all. I'll keep sending money for the fees. But I need to keep a little every month for myself, for this course.'
She was quiet. Then she said, 'Ankita, why didn't you tell us sooner?'

qa.q: What came for Ankita last week?
qa.a: The admission letter for the evening design course.

qa.q: What two feelings hit Ankita on the bus, and why?
qa.a: Ankita felt a flash of resentment, 'why is it always me', and then guilt for thinking that about the people who raised Ankita.

qa.q: What choice did Ankita make on the call with Maa?
qa.a: Instead of saying 'all fine', Ankita kept paying for the fees but clearly set aside a little each month for the course.

qa.q: How might Maa feel hearing about the course only now?
qa.a: Maa might feel sad that Ankita carried this in silence, and perhaps relieved to finally know what Ankita wants.

grounding: Shows a young adult who sends money home and delays their own wants, feels resentment and guilt together, and names a clear limit.

passage:
I've shared a room with Anjali at the working women's hostel for two years, so I know her Sunday routine. Video call with her parents at nine. Money transfer at ten. Then she goes quiet for hours.
She has been saving for a scooter since last Diwali. Last Sunday her brother asked for more money for a new phone, and I watched her say 'of course' in a bright voice and then press her forehead against the cupboard after the call.
I don't know exactly what she felt. It looked like love and anger fighting.
On Monday she asked me, 'Gopika, is it wrong to say no sometimes?' I said I didn't think so.
That night I heard her on the phone, voice shaky but clear: 'I'll send for the fees. Not for the phone. I need to keep something for me too.'

qa.q: What has Anjali been saving for since last Diwali?
qa.a: A scooter.

qa.q: What did Anjali pressing her forehead against the cupboard suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggested she was holding back hurt and anger after saying 'of course' to her brother, torn between love and resentment.

qa.q: What choice did Anjali make on the phone that night?
qa.a: She kept sending money for the fees but said no to the phone, clearly saying she needed to keep something for herself.

qa.q: How might Anjali's brother react to hearing 'Not for the phone'?
qa.a: He might feel disappointed or surprised at first, but a calm, clear limit could also help him see what his sister has been carrying.

grounding: Shows, through a roommate's eyes, a young adult who supports her family while delaying her own wants, feels love and resentment together, and sets a clear limit.

passage:
January: Tushar sent most of his salary home again, for his sister's fees and the roof repair. That night he cancelled dinner with his colleague Zainab, because by the twentieth his money had run out. He felt proud and, underneath, bitter.
March: His mother called asking for money for a cousin's wedding. Tushar said yes, then sat on the metro stairs, hating himself for resenting her.
May: He called home and said, gently, "I love you all. I'll keep paying the fees. But I can't cover weddings too. I need to build my own life." His mother went quiet, then said, "We didn't know." He felt lighter, and guilty, and both were okay.

qa.q: What did Tushar's salary pay for in January?
qa.a: His sister's fees and the roof repair.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling on the metro stairs?
qa.a: He felt resentful of his mother's request and guilty for resenting her.

qa.q: What helped Tushar most?
qa.a: Telling his family clearly and kindly what he would and wouldn't cover.

qa.q: How might his mother feel hearing "We didn't know"?
qa.a: She seems surprised and a little hurt, but also understanding once he spoke plainly.

grounding: Shows over months a young adult sending money home with love, resentment and guilt, and easing it by talking clearly about limits.

subtype: Loyalty to family versus honesty with self [Actor]
passage: Anand, you've been sending everything home, haven't you? I can see it in your lunch box. Let me tell you. At twenty-four I was a clerk in Kolkata, and every rupee went to my village: my brothers' schooling, my father's debts, my sister's wedding. I loved them. I also, secretly, hated opening my wallet. Then I hated myself for hating it. One Eid I went home and my brother asked for a motorcycle. Something in me snapped, and I shouted. My mother sat me down afterwards. That night I, Tanvir, finally said it plainly: "I'll pay for schooling. Not motorcycles. I need to build my own home too." They were hurt for a month. Then they understood. Love can have a limit, you know. Mine did, and it survived.

qa.q: What did Tanvir's brother ask for that Eid?
qa.a: A motorcycle.

qa.q: What was young Tanvir feeling about sending every rupee home?
qa.a: Tanvir loved the family but secretly resented it, and then felt guilty for resenting it.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: After the shouting at Eid, Tanvir calmly told the family what would and wouldn't be paid for.

qa.q: How did the family react to Tanvir's limit?
qa.a: They were hurt for a month, then understood.

grounding: Shows a young adult loving and resenting the duty to send money home, and finding relief in a clear limit.

passage: The job offer from Singapore had a one-week deadline, and it arrived the same day Kalyani's father's shop flooded in the Chennai rains. For three years she had sent half her salary home and paid her brother Hrithik's college fees, and she had done it gladly, mostly. Now, standing in the soggy shop with a bucket, she felt guilty for even wanting to go, and a hot resentment she couldn't say out loud. That night Hrithik found her on the terrace. "Akka, you're thinking of not taking it because of us." She didn't answer. "Talk to Appa. Tell him what you want." Next morning, over coffee, she did: she'd take the job and keep paying Hrithik's final year, and the family would decide together, with the bank's advice, how to fix the shop.

qa.q: How long was the deadline on the Singapore offer?
qa.a: One week.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling in the flooded shop?
qa.a: She felt guilty for wanting to go and a hot resentment she couldn't say out loud.

qa.q: What did Kalyani's talk with Appa achieve?
qa.a: It set a clear limit: she'd take the job and pay Hrithik's final year, while the shop became a shared family decision with proper advice.

qa.q: How does Hrithik see his sister's sacrifice?
qa.a: Hrithik sees she's putting the family first and encourages her to say what she wants.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult torn between family duty and her own opportunity, easing guilt and resentment by stating limits clearly.

subtype: Loyalty to family versus honesty with self [Actor]
passage:
Every month, on the first, Irfan transferred most of his salary home from his Bengaluru office. Abbu's shop had closed during the lockdown, and his younger sister, Dilnaz, was in college.
He loved them. He was proud he could do it. But the design course he'd wanted for three years was still just a saved link. He'd skipped his friend's wedding in Goa to save the fare.
Last Sunday, on the video call, Ammi said, "Beta, the neighbour's son bought a car."
Irfan felt something hot rise in his chest, then immediately felt guilty for it.
After the call, Dilnaz messaged him. "Bhaiya, you look tired. Are you okay?"
He typed and deleted three times. Then: "I love helping. But I need to keep some for myself too. I want to do my course. Can we talk to Ammi and Abbu together about what's possible?"
Dilnaz replied: "Yes. I'll be there."

qa.q: What did Irfan skip to save the fare?
qa.a: His friend's wedding in Goa.

qa.q: What did Irfan feel when Ammi mentioned the neighbour's son's car?
qa.a: He felt a flash of resentment, something hot rising in his chest, and then felt guilty for it.

qa.q: What step did Irfan take toward being honest with himself and his family?
qa.a: He told Dilnaz he needed to keep something for himself and his course, and asked to talk to their parents together about what's possible.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel reading Irfan's message?
qa.a: Dilnaz, who noticed he looked tired, may feel relieved he was honest and glad to support him by being there for the talk.

grounding: Shows a young adult supporting his family while delaying his own wants, feeling both love and resentment, and moving toward a clear talk about limits.
